answers.answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value store / data structure server: a network server keeping keys mapped to typed values (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams and more) primarily in RAM, with optional persistence to disk (RDB snapshots, append only file). It is meant for real-time applications where an on-disk database is too slow for the request path: caching (with eviction and key expiration), session stores, queues and messaging (job queues on lists, priority queues on sorted sets, pub/sub, streams), and search and vectors (secondary indexing, full-text and vector similarity search; vector sets in beta). Also described as a document and vector query engine.

answers.answer: The two are RDB snapshots and the append only file (AOF). RDB: serverCron checks configured save points and, when enough changes and seconds have passed, rdbSaveBackground forks a child (redisFork) that writes a dump while the parent keeps serving. AOF: feedAppendOnlyFile appends each propagated write to a memory buffer and flushAppendOnlyFile writes it to disk in beforeSleep, before replies are sent. How they differ in durability: not stated (the trade-off text is withheld because it rests on redis.conf). Which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled: not stated.

Purpose: a modules API lets developers add new commands and data types beyond the built-in ones. A module is a shared library loaded into redis-server, for example with a loadmodule line in the configuration ('loaded at startup'). Bundled external modules (search, JSON, time series, probabilistic) are cloned by make modules-update; only vector-sets is present in the clone. answers.answer: The event loop (ae.c library) sleeps until file descriptors are ready, then processes their events; aeMain repeats this until stopped. Connection layer: the listening socket's handler connSocketAcceptHandler (socket.c) accepts TCP and calls acceptCommonHandler, which creates a client; createClient installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler so the event loop calls it when bytes arrive. Client code (networking.c) fills the query buffer, processInputBuffer parses multibulk or inline commands and calls processCommandAndResetClient; processCommand checks and call runs it; replies go into the client output buffer via addReply. Before the loop waits again, beforeSleep flushes the AOF buffer (flushAppendOnlyFile) and calls handleClientsWithPendingWrites to send buffered replies. serverCron runs periodic work such as save-point checks. A full step-by-step account of one loop turn beyond this: not stated.

Slot: one of 16384 buckets, given by the CRC16 of the key's name. Serve or redirect: processCommand redirects clients whose keys are owned by another cluster node; multi-key operations work only when all keys share a slot. answers.answer: connSocketAcceptHandler accepts the connection; acceptCommonHandler creates a client; createClient sets readQueryFromClient as read handler; the event loop calls it when bytes arrive, it fills the query buffer and calls processInputBuffer, which picks multibulk (*) or inline protocol, parses arguments and calls processCommandAndResetClient. processCommand looks up the command and checks it; inside MULTI it is queued and answered QUEUED, otherwise call runs the command's proc against memory. The reply is written with addReply to the output buffer. After a write, call hands it to alsoPropagate; propagateNow feeds it to feedAppendOnlyFile (AOF buffer, flushed to disk in beforeSleep before replies are sent) and replicationFeedSlaves (replication stream). handleClientsWithPendingWrites in beforeSleep sends the replies. Checks that can stop it: command lookup, ACL permission check, cluster redirection when keys are owned by another node, eviction when maxmemory is set, and refusal of writes after a persistence error. Other checks: not stated.

A replica connects with SYNC or PSYNC, handled by syncCommand; PSYNC resumes partially when it can instead of copying everything again, and after a short disconnect the replica can resume from the replication backlog instead of a full resync. Why: a single-threaded core keeps the design simple ('threading is not a silver bullet'); many simple shared-nothing cores combined by higher-level protocols (e.g. Redis Cluster) are simpler and suit NUMA systems; memory is fast and performance predictable. Where it uses extra threads/processes: optional I/O threads (io-threads) read, parse and write sockets; background saves use a forked child; the manifesto anticipates parallelism only for I/O. Costs/conditions: maintainers suggest enabling I/O threads only on machines with at least four cores and only when there is a real performance problem; threaded I/O is not supported for TLS connections; repl-compression works only when io-threads is above 1; a single slow command delays every other client of the instance.
